slides:
SLIDE 1 — Title
Redwood Inference: Standard Demo (v1)
Subtitle: Production-grade LLM inference that’s fast, reliable, and flexible

Presenter line: AE + SE
Date/Version: Working draft (do not forward externally)

[PLACEHOLDER] Background image: Console “Routes” view w/ latency panel overlay
[DESIGN NOTE] Use new template (DES-311) once finalized.

[COMMENT - Stephanie N.] Make it clear in first 10 seconds: “Why Redwood vs. just calling an API?”
[COMMENT - Markus K.] Add the 2-minute “Hosted mini-demo” path callout early; AEs keep asking.
SLIDE 2 — What you’ll see today (choose-your-own-adventure)
Option A (default, 18–22 min):
- 1) Fast, predictable inference (streaming)
- 2) Reliability: routing + fallback in production
- 3) Cost controls: caching/batching + quantization profiles
- 4) Observability: token cost, latency, errors
- 5) Deployment modes: Hosted → Dedicated → Private

Option B (fast path, 6–8 min):
- Live API call + 1 Console proof point + next steps

[Speaker note] Ask: “What matters most: latency, reliability, cost, or security?” Then pick order.

[COMMENT - Soojin L.] Need a single line: “Everything you see is running on our demo tenant with pinned versions + dashboards.”
SLIDE 3 — Persona prompts (internal-only)
Platform/Infra Eng:
- “How do I keep p95 stable under load?”
- “How do I roll models safely?”

ML Eng:
- “How do I keep quality stable while reducing cost?”
- “How do I evaluate regressions?”

Security/Compliance:
- “Where does data go? How long is it retained?”
- “Can I run this privately in VPC/on-prem?”

Procurement/IT:
- “What’s the commercial path from pilot to steady state capacity?”

[Speaker note] This slide is optional; hide for external-facing deck.
[COMMENT - Markus K.] Keep, but mark as “Appendix / presenter view only.”
SLIDE 4 — The problem: LLMs are easy to try, hard to serve
- Inference is where cost + UX lives
- Traffic is spiky; sequence lengths are messy
- Model updates can break prompts
- Reliability needs fallbacks and clear blast radius

Proof points we’ll show live:
- Streaming UX
- Route policy + fallback
- Cost/latency breakdowns

[PLACEHOLDER] Simple diagram: App → Inference Layer → GPUs (multi-region)
[COMMENT - Marissa C.] Avoid “hard to serve” sounding like fear. Use “hard to make predictable.”
SLIDE 5 — What Redwood provides (one slide mental model)
Redwood Inference = unified runtime + control plane for production inference
- Hosted API: fastest start
- Dedicated: reserved capacity + isolation
- Private: VPC/on-prem options for regulated workloads

Plus:
- Console: dashboards, rollouts, tracing hooks
- Optimize: cost/perf recommendations

[PLACEHOLDER] Product surface diagram (Hosted/Dedicated/Private stacked)
[COMMENT - Lukas M.] Add “EU region support” footnote but avoid hard commitments; use “regional deployment options.”
SLIDE 6 — Demo tenant disclaimer (internal)
This demo uses a sanitized demo tenant:
- No customer data; seeded sample prompts only
- Pinned model versions + quant profiles for repeatability
- Guardrails: quotas/rate limits to avoid runaway usage

If something fails live:
- Switch to “Plan B” canned responses + screenshots
- Route to backup model profile

[Speaker note] Don’t dwell; 10–15 seconds max.
[COMMENT - Naomi F.] Add one bullet: “Logging is configured to avoid storing raw prompts by default in demo tenant.”
SLIDE 7 — Scenario 1: Streaming chat (UX + latency)
Goal: Show “fast token streaming” and stable p95 behavior.

Live steps:
1) Run a streaming request (curl or small client)
2) Highlight first-token latency + tokens/sec
3) Jump to Console latency chart for that route

[PLACEHOLDER] Screenshot: Console → Requests/Tracing view showing stream timeline
[COMMENT - Markus K.] Keep the prompt short. Use a deterministic, non-controversial prompt (no “write an essay”).
SLIDE 8 — Live demo: Streaming request (copy/paste)
Command (Hosted API):
- curl https://api.redwood.example/v1/chat.completions \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $DEMO_API_KEY" \
  -d '{"model":"rw-chat-v3.2-pinned","stream":true,"messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Summarize this product requirement in 4 bullets..."}]}'

Expected:
- Response begins streaming in < 1s (range statement only)
- No UI freezes; steady throughput

[Presenter note] If Wi-Fi is bad, switch to pre-recorded terminal output clip.

[COMMENT - Stephanie N.] Remove any specific numeric latency unless approved by “Benchmark Proof Points” doc.
[COMMENT - Soojin L.] Add “safe language” banner: “Latency varies by region/model; we’ll show relative improvements + controls.”
SLIDE 9 — What makes it predictable (high-level, no deep kernel talk)
Redwood runtime focuses on:
- Continuous batching tuned for real traffic
- KV cache management + prefix caching
- Hardware-aware execution + quantization-friendly paths

What you get:
- Better unit economics without rewriting your app
- Stability knobs: route policies, quotas, fallbacks

[PLACEHOLDER] Diagram: Requests → smart batching/caching → GPU execution
[COMMENT - Simran K.] Keep “KV cache” but define it verbally (e.g., “reusing context work”).
SLIDE 10 — Scenario 2: Reliability via routing + fallback
Goal: Show graceful degradation under constraints.

Live steps:
1) Open Console → Routes
2) Show primary model pinned to version
3) Show fallback model(s) and trigger conditions
4) Simulate failure mode (capacity constraint / forced error)
5) Show request succeeding via fallback with annotation

[PLACEHOLDER] Screenshot: Route policy panel with fallback chain
[COMMENT - Markus K.] We need a “safe” failure that won’t look scary: prefer forced 429 or forced “simulate capacity” toggle vs. actual outage.
SLIDE 11 — Live demo: Route policy (what to point at)
Callouts to narrate:
- Route name: “demo-standard-chat”
- Policy: latency tier / region preference
- Fallback chain: rw-chat-v3.2-pinned → rw-chat-v3.2-lite → rw-chat-v3.1-backup
- Logging: fallback reason recorded

[Speaker note] The win: app stays online even when capacity changes.

[COMMENT - Marissa C.] Make sure UI labels match current Console (PR-22031 renamed “Fallback” section).
SLIDE 12 — Scenario 3: Cost controls (caching/batching/quant profiles)
Goal: Show cost levers with observability.

What we’ll show:
- Prefix cache hit rate improves $/request for repeated prompts
- Batch settings increase throughput under load
- Quantization profile reduces cost while monitoring quality

[PLACEHOLDER] Screenshot: Optimize panel w/ “recommendation” cards
[COMMENT - Renee S.] Keep this grounded: show “token cost breakdown” before/after instead of claiming % savings.
SLIDE 13 — Live demo: Token cost + latency breakdown
Console views to open:
- Cost dashboard (token-level)
- Latency breakdown by stage (queue vs inference)
- Cache panel (hit/miss)

Narration:
- “Here’s where you’re paying”
- “Here’s what changed when we enabled caching / adjusted batching”

[PLACEHOLDER] Dashboard export (observability-pack/pr-477)
[COMMENT - Logan W.] Ensure demo dashboard has stable queries; we had missing panels in earlier imports.
SLIDE 14 — Scenario 4: Structured output + tool calling (developer experience)
Goal: Show app integration patterns + reliability of structured responses.

Live steps (pick one):
A) Structured JSON output for an extraction task
B) Tool calling: model calls a function, then returns final response

[PLACEHOLDER] Screenshot: Example response JSON + schema
[COMMENT - Markus K.] Tool calling demo is high risk if model deviates; structured output is safer. Keep tool calling optional.
SLIDE 15 — “Known-good” scripts (reproducibility)
We maintain demo scripts so anyone can run the same scenarios:
- Curl + SDK examples
- Canned inputs
- Expected outputs (tolerances for nondeterminism)
- Weekly regression check before field rollout

References:
- redwood-examples PR-842
- ENG-4923 weekly scenario check

[COMMENT - Soojin L.] Add an internal link placeholder: “Demo Scenarios - Known Good Matrix” sheet.
SLIDE 16 — Observability: what your team gets day 2
What teams care about after week 1:
- Per-route/model dashboards
- Error analysis + fallback reasons
- Rollouts with canary + automatic fallback
- Tracing hooks (bring your own APM)

[PLACEHOLDER] Screenshot: Errors panel with “fallback invoked” annotation
[COMMENT - Stephanie N.] Tie this to business outcome: “Fewer incident calls / less guesswork.”
SLIDE 17 — Safe rollouts (model versioning + blast radius)
Key ideas:
- Pin model versions for stability
- Canary route changes
- A/B tests with eval harness (when relevant)
- Automatic rollback / fallback policies

[PLACEHOLDER] Screenshot: Rollout timeline view
[COMMENT - Simran K.] Mention “prompt set regression alerts” only if we can show it or confidently describe current capability.
SLIDE 18 — Deployment flexibility (Hosted → Dedicated → Private)
Same interface, different deployment mode:
- Hosted API: fastest start, usage-based
- Dedicated: reserved capacity, predictable throughput, isolation
- Private: VPC/on-prem, customer-managed networking

[Speaker note] This is the “you don’t have to replatform later” slide.

[PLACEHOLDER] Diagram: single API surface across three boxes
[COMMENT - Lukas M.] Add a small callout: “Data residency / region routing available depending on deployment.”
SLIDE 19 — Dedicated: when it’s the right move
Triggers we see:
- Sustained throughput needs
- Data isolation requirements
- Performance SLOs (p95) with predictable capacity

What you get:
- Dedicated GPU pool
- SLA-backed targets (discuss ranges verbally)
- Autoscaling policies + burst options

[COMMENT - Stephanie N.] Keep SLAs vague in deck; handle details in Q&A.
SLIDE 20 — Private (VPC/on-prem): for regulated workloads
Common reasons:
- Network controls + private endpoints
- Audit log requirements
- KMS/HSM integrations
- Air-gapped or on-prem constraints

What we can say safely:
- “We support VPC/private control plane options”
- “We can align retention/logging to policy” (avoid exact numbers on slide)

[COMMENT - Naomi F.] Add “SSO/SAML/RBAC supported” only if consistent with current enterprise features.
SLIDE 21 — Security posture (demo-safe summary)
High-level commitments (no sensitive details in deck):
- Encryption in transit + at rest
- Access controls (RBAC)
- Audit logging available (deployment dependent)
- Data handling: customer controls vary by mode

[PLACEHOLDER] Link badge: “Demo Tenant Security FAQ”

[COMMENT - Naomi F.] Add disclaimer: “Details available under NDA / security package.”
[COMMENT - Markus K.] Keep this short; the FAQ is where we go deep.
SLIDE 22 — Competitive framing (what we show vs what we claim)
What we show live:
- Streaming + latency charts
- Fallback routing behavior
- Token cost breakdown
- Dashboarding + error analysis

What we claim (with proof points available on request):
- Better production economics via batching/caching/quant profiles
- Reliability via fallbacks + pinned versions + rollouts
- Deployment flexibility without API churn

[Speaker note] Avoid naming competitors on slide; handle in Q&A.

[COMMENT - Camila R.] Ensure wording matches approved messaging; no “cheaper than X” statements.
SLIDE 23 — Next steps (turn demo into evaluation)
Recommended next steps:
1) Pick one workload (route) and success metric (latency/cost/quality)
2) Share traffic shape assumptions (RPS, seq lengths)
3) Run a 1–2 week evaluation plan

What we provide:
- Quickstart template + scripts
- Security FAQ + security package process
- Support channel + weekly check-ins
